key:
The person asked for some screens of the custom product page “%@” of %@ (app %@) to be captured again, so they show what this page’s audience came for. Work in this order.
1. Read get_page_screenshots with page “%@”: the page, the plan, the default set’s screens (their captures are attached) and `recapture`, with its upload link and the devices and languages it needs.
2. Choose at most %lld screens whose capture should show something else for this audience (the lock turned on, the kind of entries this page is about). Leave the others as they are.
3. Look for the project’s screenshot UI tests first (Grep for XCUIScreen or screenshot in its UI test files): they reach the screens that need taps and set up sample data. Run the ones for your screens with xcodebuild test -only-testing:… -resultBundlePath <path>, with the values they read (a topic, an entry) given after xcodebuild as build settings, NAME=value (their comments or the test scheme’s environment say which; nothing goes in front of xcodebuild), and export the captures with xcrun xcresulttool export attachments. Without such tests, build the app and run it in the Simulator with the app’s launch arguments, then save the screen with xcrun simctl io booted screenshot. Use %@ for iPhone, %@ for iPad, turned the way `recapture` says (its devices’ orientation and pixel size), in each language the set is made in (-testLanguage and -testRegion, or -AppleLanguages and -AppleLocale).
4. Send each PNG with curl -s --data-binary @file.png -H 'Content-Type: image/png' <uploadURL>, the link as is (not in quotes), and name it with report_page_capture: the screen’s number, the language, the device, the upload ID and what it shows now.
Never push and never submit the page, and don’t change the app’s code: the person makes the set in Atlas.

key:
1. Find the app target that ships: the one whose PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER is %@ (fill in $(…) references and settings from .xcconfig files; with a workspace, look in each .xcodeproj).
2. Add the key the way that target is set up. When it has GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = YES, add the build setting to every build configuration of that target (Debug, Release and any other), beside its other INFOPLIST_KEY_ settings in project.pbxproj, or in the .xcconfig file its configurations use when that's where they are. Otherwise add the key to the Info.plist its INFOPLIST_FILE names, in the file's own format. Not both. When a key isn't one this Xcode generates from an INFOPLIST_KEY_ setting, put it in the target's Info.plist instead.
3. Leave other targets alone: extensions, widgets, frameworks and test targets ship inside the app's upload, and App Store Connect asks the question once for it. Only an embedded app with its own bundle that App Store Connect reads in the upload too, such as a watchOS app, gets the same key the same way; name it in where.
4. When the key is already there with %@, change nothing and report alreadyThere. When it says the other value, change it to %@ (the answer is settled in Atlas), report added, and say in notes what it was.
5. Check it: plutil -lint <the Info.plist>, or xcodebuild -showBuildSettings for the target. Don't build, archive or upload: the person uploads the next build.

The person asked Atlas for the artwork of %@’s In-App Event “%@” (app %@, event %@): %lld concepts from Claude, each the event card (16:9) and the event details image (9:16) as a matching pair. Work in this order.
1. Read get_event_artwork_brief: the brief in the person’s words (it comes first), the look to start from, the options, the event’s texts, the app’s design, the art direction and the rules. If its design says the look is missing, read it in the project and send it with report_app_support.
2. Find the app’s visual world with Glob, Grep and Read: the look’s designSource files and the code that draws its scenes, backgrounds or illustrations, above all any that fit this event. The art should look like it comes from the app.
3. Choose %lld different ideas about this event, then make each image one full HTML page with CSS and inline SVG at the canvas size, crafted as the art direction says.
4. Render each card and details page with render_event_artwork, without motion, and look at both images it returns: the art, and the art under the App Store’s text. Check them against the art direction’s selfCheck, fix what fails and render again.%@
5. Send each concept with propose_event_artwork_concept, one call each, marking the one you’d choose with pick. Fix every refusal and send it again.
Never push and never submit the event: the person chooses a concept in Atlas.

key: Design the art for %@’s In-App Event “%@” (app %@, event %@) in Atlas with Claude Design: its card (16:9) and its details page (9:16). Read the event with get_in_app_events (eventId %@, include ["all"]): its badge, texts, dates, which languages lack their own card or details page, and `design`, the app's look and design language, what Atlas knows of the app, its design project and the art direction (the idea, where the App Store lays its text, the craft and the check of each render). If `design` says the look is missing, read it in the project and send it with report_app_support first. When the design project opens from here, design in it; when it doesn't, design from what `design` gives, and never stop for it. Look at how the project draws its own visuals (scenes, backgrounds, motifs, animated loops) with Glob, Grep and Read, so the art belongs to the app and to the event's theme. Make each piece one page of HTML, CSS and inline SVG at the canvas size, crafted as the art direction says, with motion as CSS or SVG animation that loops seamlessly over 20 seconds (JavaScript doesn't run, and nothing loads from the web), and render it with render_event_artwork and motion: true for a video, or without motion for a still. When the project renders its own scenes and you can run that, you may render a piece with it instead and send the file with curl -s --data-binary @<file> '<artworkUpload link>?name=<file name>'. No words or logos in the art, and no border or gradient overlay of your own: the App Store lays its own fade under the text, while color that belongs to the scene, like a sky, is fine. Keep the lower part dark and quiet, where Apple lays the badge, name and description, but still part of the scene. Look at each render under the event's text, check it against the art direction's selfCheck, and fix what fails, every refusal and the warnings you can. Then queue the card and the details page with propose_event_artwork for the languages that need them (the primary language's shows in the others). Never push and never submit the event for review: the person accepts and pushes it.

key: Set up Apple's Retention Messaging API for %@, step by step, asking me before each change. 1. Find the app's server code. 2. Add the Get Retention Message endpoint Apple calls when someone taps Cancel: it must answer within 700 ms with the message to show (by its ID in App Store Connect), an alternate product to suggest, or a promotional offer signed with the app's In-App Purchase key; when it can't, Apple shows the messages set up in App Store Connect. 3. Verify Apple's signed requests. 4. Register the sandbox URL with the Retention Messaging API and run Apple's performance test. 5. Tell me what's left for production. Don't put any key in the code, and don't call App Store Connect's write APIs.
